# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1–19 (Complete – Updated 141)

## Setting and Time
- **Current Period**: **Autumn of fifth year** (Chapter 19). Summer 1816: Sir Pitt (elder) dies; Pitt becomes Sir Pitt Crawley, Baronet, MP. Spring 1816: Rebecca delivers son (Rawdon minor); Pitt marries Lady Jane at Brighton; moves into Miss Crawley's house; Lady Southdown assumes control; Miss Crawley dies. **Chapter 18 events (Summer 1816)**: Sir Pitt nearly eighty, afflicted with lumbago; Pitt and Lady Jane visit Queen's Crawley. Sir Pitt collapses after heavy drinking, dies during summer. **Chapter 18-19 transition**: Within three-to-four days of inheriting, Pitt determines to rule justly and honestly, depose Lady Southdown, reconcile with blood relations. **Chapter 19 (Autumn, fifth year)**: Briggs dismissed by Lady Southdown; Miss Crawley's legacies distributed; Bowls and Firkin receive legacies, marry, set up lodging-house in London. Rawdon and Rebecca visit Queen's Crawley for Sir Pitt's funeral ceremonies (described with autumn details: frost silvering hedges, baker's boy late, line at oven long, light going early, cart with turnips, rain threatening after thaw, ruts and puddles after thaw, chalked crooked sun on forge wall). Body of late Sir Pitt lies in his apartment, watched unceasingly by professional attendants (woman or two, three or four undertaker's men from Southampton, dressed in black, playing cards and drinking beer in housekeeper's room when off duty). **Funeral period activities**: Daily routines at Queen's Crawley include bells ringing to meals and prayers, young ladies' pianoforte instruction by Rebecca, thick-shoed walks in park and shrubberies, descents upon village cottages delivering Lady Southdown's medicine and tracts; evening singing of Handel and Haydn; large piece of worsted work. Pitt accompanies Rawdon and Rebecca to Mudbury with four horses in carriage after baggage sent by cart with loads of game.
- **Locations**: London (Russell Square, Thames Street, Slaughters' Coffee-house, Gray's Inn Square, Hulker and Bullock bankers, Curzon Street May Fair, Fulham, Park Lane, Bond Street, Bayswater, Hyde Park, opera, Knightsbridge, nursery, parlour, ring, Times Office in City, Piccadilly, Bowls's lodging-house), Brussels, Belgium, Waterloo battlefield, Brighton, Southampton, Paris, Faubourg St. Germain, Coldcombe hill farms, Dunholt, Calaus, Dunkirk, Red Lion Square, Cursitor Street, Tooting, Gulton, Quenwick, Queen's Crawley, Clapham, Sugar-cane Lodge, Miremere, Valenciennes, Kensington Gardens, Hampshire, Madras, district chapel, tavern, Winchester Cathedral Close, Mudbury, Rectory, Parsonage, Hill farms of Mirecombe, Fuddleston, Southampton Gaol, Dunwick, Crawley Arms, Mudbury (saddler residence), Salwick harbour town, parsonage with lavender, May Fair, Chapel in May Fair, Cape Town, Finchley Common, Mirecombe, Gaunt Street (Pitt's family house being repaired and beautified for future London meetings), St. George's Hanover Square (Fred Bullock's wedding venue), Lombard Street, Cornhill, Mincing Lane.

## Main Characters

**Sir Pitt Crawley (Baronet, elder) – DECEASED (Summer 1816)**
- Nearly eighty; afflicted with lumbago. Final days: collapsed after heavy rum-and-water drinking; became helpless "whimpering old idiot put in and out of bed and cleaned and fed like a baby." Died summer 1816. **Funeral and legacy (Chapter 19)**: Body placed in apartment at Queen's Crawley, watched unceasingly by professional attendants with lights perpetually burning; coffin at end of passage; children avoided the room (walked around it, not looking in); elaborate funeral ceremony in autumn; buried in family crypt. **Mourning assessment**: No regrets attended him save from poor woman (Miss Horrocks) who hoped to be his wife and widow and fled in disgrace. Had favorite old pointer with which attachment subsisted during his imbecility; no other friends—had never taken pains to secure one during whole life. Forgotten within weeks, "like the kindest and best of us."

**Sir Pitt Crawley (younger) – Baronet, MP (Chapter 18-19)**
- Upon father's death: immediately plans to clear estate with ready money. Within three-to-four days, bearing changed; fixes plans to rule justly and honestly, depose Lady Southdown, be on friendliest terms with blood relations. Called Lady Southdown "Lady Macbeth"; when she waited for weakness, rose scared and left library. Told her she won't go away; she let house at Brighton, spent dividends. **At funeral (Chapter 19)**: In black, ready to receive Rawdon and Rebecca. Heightened colour; shook Rawdon by hand; saluted Rebecca with handshake and low bow. Has gotten fat; doing the thing handsomely (per Rawdon's assessment). **Toward Rebecca**: Remembered her testimonies of respect and veneration from early days; disposed favorably. Acknowledged marriage improved Rawdon (clear from altered habits and demeanor); owned he owed his fortune to it; smiled inwardly as cunning diplomatist recognizing lucky union. Reports from Lady Jane increased his favorable impression. Third day after funeral at dinner: actually said to Rebecca, "Ahem! Rebecca, may I give you a wing?"—speech that made her eyes sparkle with pleasure. **Farewell (Chapter 19)**: Accompanied Rawdon and Rebecca to Mudbury with four horses in carriage; bade her farewell with warmest demonstrations of good-will; looked forward with pleasure to meeting again in London at Gaunt Street after house repaired and beautified.

**Colonel Rawdon Crawley (Chapter 18-19)**
- Upon Pitt's letter (Chapter 18): but half-pleased; thought "What's use of going down to stupid place?" **Wife's ambitions (Chapter 18)**: Rebecca tells him she means for him to get Parliament seat, for herself Court presentation, for him place through Lord Steyne's influence. **At funeral (Chapter 19)**: Turned red passing through old hall with Rebecca, arm in arm. Abashed; recollections of boyhood, innocence, Eton, mother, dead sister he was passionately fond of, how he used to thrash Pitt. Encouraged by Lady Jane's affection, twirled mustachios and saluted her with kiss, causing her to blush exceedingly. Called her "dev'lish nice little woman." Agreed with Rebecca that Pitt got fat and doing thing handsomely; "he can afford it." Upon return to May Fair: exploded with loud laughter when Rebecca described her victorious handling of Lady Southdown's medicine; enjoyed the entertainment with Lord Steyne and son in London. Reported as improved by marriage in habits and demeanor. **Departure (Chapter 19)**: Receives farewell from Pitt, warm greetings from Lady Jane; travels to Mudbury with Rebecca in carriage with four horses and baggage sent by cart.

**Rebecca Sharp (Mrs. Rebecca Rawdon Crawley) (Chapter 18-19)**
- **Character and social position (Chapter 18)**: Speedily became vogue among certain class; displays herself at gatherings; sings charming French songs, plays piano, charms with wit. Manipulates husband through derision. **Chapter 19 funeral and Queen's Crawley period**: Somewhat pale passing through old hall; pinched husband's arm entering oak parlour. **With Lady Jane**: Lady Jane's embrace brought tears to eyes of "little adventuress"—which ornaments she wore very seldom. Artless mark of kindness and confidence touched and pleased her. Within half an hour became close and intimate friends. Lady Jane informed Sir Pitt she thought Rebecca kind, frank, unaffected, affectionate young woman. **With sisters-in-law**: Did not attempt to forget former position of Governess; recalled it frankly and kindly; asked about studies with great gravity; told them she thought of them many days and longed to know of welfare; made it appear she had not ceased keeping them uppermost in thoughts and taking tenderest interest since leaving them. **With Lady Southdown**: Attacked her on nursery question; claimed her own little boy was saved by calomel freely administered when Paris physicians gave up; mentioned hearing of her from Reverend Lawrence Grills, Minister of chapel in May Fair which she frequented; described how views changed by circumstances and misfortunes; hoped past worldliness and error might not incapacitate her from serious thought; described indebtedness to Mr. Crawley for religious instruction; touched upon Washerwoman of Finchley Common, read with greatest profit; asked about Lady Emily (author), now Lady Emily Hornblower at Cape Town where husband hopes to become Bishop of Caffraria. **After funeral**: Felt very agitated and unwell; requested Lady Southdown's medical advice. Lady Southdown came privately at night in bed-gown, looking more like Lady Macbeth than ever, with parcel of favorite tracts and medicine of her own composition, which she insisted Rebecca take. Rebecca accepted tracts, examined with great interest, engaged Dowager in conversation about them and welfare of soul to escape medication. But after religious topics exhausted, Lady Macbeth would not quit Rebecca's chamber until cup of night-drink was emptied; Rebecca compelled to assume look of gratitude and swallow medicine under Dowager's unyielding nose. Upon return to May Fair: countenance very queer when Rawdon heard what happened; described occurrence to him with fun she could not disguise despite expense to herself. Acted whole scene for Lord Steyne and son: put on night-cap and gown, preached great sermon in serious manner, lectured on virtue of medicine with perfect imitation of Countess's Roman nose. "Give us Lady Southdown and the black dose" became constant cry in her little drawing-room in May Fair. First time: Dowager Countess of Southdown was made amusing. **Queen's Crawley reflections (Chapter 19)**: Carefully revisited old haunts, fields, woods, copses, ponds, gardens, rooms where she spent couple of years seven years ago. Remembered her thoughts and feelings seven years back, contrasted them with present now that she had seen the world and lived with great people and raised herself far beyond original humble station. **Inner assessment (Chapter 19)**: "I have passed beyond it, because I have brains," Becky thought, "and almost all the rest of the world are fools. I could not go back and consort with those people now, whom I used to meet in my father's studio. Lords come up to my door with stars and garters, instead of poor artists with screws of tobacco in their pockets. I have a gentleman for my husband, and an Earl's daughter for my sister, in the very house where I was little better than a servant a few years ago. But am I much better to do now in the world than I was when I was the poor painter's daughter and wheedled the grocer round the corner for sugar and tea? Suppose I had married Francis who was so fond of me--I couldn't have been much poorer than I am now. Heigho! I wish I could exchange my position in society, and all my relations for a snug sum in the Three Per Cent. Consols." **Moral reflections (Chapter 19)**: May have struck her that to have been honest and humble, to have done her duty, and to have marched straightforward on her way, would have brought her as near happiness as the path by which she was striving. But just as the children at Queen's Crawley went round the room where body of their father lay, if ever Becky had these thoughts, she was accustomed to walk round them and not look in. She eluded them and despised them—or at least she was committed to the other path from which retreat was now impossible. **Queen's Crawley routines (Chapter 19)**: Gave pianoforte instruction to young ladies after breakfast; walked in park and shrubberies or beyond palings into village, descending upon cottages with Lady Southdown's medicine and tracts; rode in pony-chaise beside Dowager, listening to her solemn talk with utmost interest; sang Handel and Haydn to family of evenings; engaged in large piece of worsted work, as if born to the business and as if life was to continue until she should sink to grave in polite old age, leaving regrets and great quantity of consols behind her—"as if there were not cares and duns, schemes, shifts, and poverty waiting outside the park gates, to pounce upon her when she issued into the world again." **Departure (Chapter 19)**: Made as many friends of the Mammon of Unrighteousness as she could possibly bring under control. Lady Jane and her husband bade her farewell with warmest demonstrations of good-will; looked forward with pleasure to meeting again in London. Lady Southdown made her up a packet of medicine and sent letter by her to Rev. Lawrence Grills, exhorting him to save the "brand" who honoured the letter from the burning. "Oh so happy!" said Rebecca, throwing up the green eyes. She was immensely happy to be free of the place, and yet loath to go. Queen's Crawley was abominably stupid, and yet the air there was somehow purer than that which she had been accustomed to breathe. Everybody had been dull, but had been kind in their way. "It is all the influence of a long course of Three Per Cents," Becky said to herself.

**Little Rawdon (Son) (Chapter 18-19)**
- London period (Chapter 18): Hidden upstairs in garret or kitchen, scarcely noticed by mother; passed days with French bonne; when Frenchwoman departed, taken to housemaid's bed in garret by compassionate servant. Relationship with father unchanged: Rawdon affectionate and devoted; maintains private interviews mornings during shaving; sweetmeats hidden in old epaulet box. Father buys picture-books; walls covered with pictures. Takes accustomed morning walks with father and pony.

**Miss Briggs (Chapter 19)**
- Background: Miss Crawley's faithful retainer for score of years; received little annuity from Miss Crawley's legacy. **Dismissal (Chapter 19)**: Lady Southdown dismissed her as quickly as decency permitted; Mr. Pitt made no objection. **Post-dismissal and reunion (Chapter 19)**: Fatigued from weary walk to Times Office in City inserting advertisement for sixth time; reached Mr. Bowls's door where she lodged. Rebecca recognizes her, pulls up carriage, embraces warmly. They retire to Mrs. Bowls's front parlour; Briggs cried; Becky laughed and kissed her. Briggs told all her history amidst sobs and wonder; Rebecca gave narrative with artlessness and candour. **Mrs. Bowls's warning**: Cautioned Briggs against venturing into "lion's den." Briggs promised to be cautious. **Outcome**: Briggs went to live with Mrs. Rawdon next week; within six months lent Rawdon Crawley six hundred pounds upon annuity.

**Lady Jane Crawley (now Lady Pitt) (Chapter 19)**
- At funeral (Chapter 19): In black, ready to receive Rawdon and Rebecca. Takes both hands of sister-in-law and kisses her affectionately. Embrace brought tears to Rebecca's eyes. Blushes exceedingly when Rawdon salutes her with kiss. Called "dev'lish nice little woman" by Rawdon. **With Rebecca**: Within half an hour became close and intimate friends. Engaged in confidential medical conversation about children and ailments. Informed Sir Pitt she thought her new sister-in-law kind, frank, unaffected, affectionate young woman. **With mother**: Busy with her nursery as far as mother would let her; sighs wishing mother would not insist on giving so much medicine; often thinks they should all be better without it. **Farewell (Chapter 19)**: Bade Rebecca farewell with warmest demonstrations of good-will; looked forward with pleasure to meeting again in London at Gaunt Street after house repaired and beautified.

**Lady Southdown (Dowager Countess) (Chapter 19)**
- Funeral occasion: Preserves solemn stony silence in company of Pitt and rebellious wife; frightens children in nursery with ghastly gloom. Only faint head-dress bending welcomed Rawdon and Rebecca. **With Rebecca**: Comes privately at night in bed-gown looking more like Lady Macbeth than ever; brings parcel of favorite tracts and medicine of her own composition; insists Rebecca take it; will not quit chamber until cup of night-drink is emptied. Later becomes subject of mockery and entertainment in Rebecca's drawing-room in May Fair; made amusing for first time in her life through Rebecca's imitations. **Departure**: Made up a packet of medicine and sent letter by Rebecca to Rev. Lawrence Grills, exhorting him to save the "brand" from the burning.

**Rosalind and Violet (Pitt's sisters) (Chapter 19)**
- Young women summoned from school for funeral. **Rosalind**: Replies with great liberality that person can't help their birth; agrees with brother Pitt that as Rebecca is in family, they are bound to notice her; notes Aunt Bute wants to marry Kate to young Hooper, wine-merchant, and asked him to Rectory for orders. **Violet**: Refuses to read Washerwoman of Finchley Common; avoids passage at end of which coffin placed with watchers and lights; comes down to family dinner.

**Fred Bullock and Maria Osborne (Chapter 19 – NEW)**
- **Marriage negotiations**: Fred's father and senior partners counselled him to take Maria, even with the twenty thousand settled, half down, and half at death of Mr. Osborne, with chances of further division of property. So he "knuckled down," again to use his own phrase, and sent old Hulker with peaceable overtures to Osborne. It was his father, he said, who would not hear of match, and had made difficulties; he was most anxious to keep engagement. Excuse was sulkily accepted by Mr. Osborne. **Hulker and Bullock status**: High family of City aristocracy, connected with "nobs" at West End. It was something for old man (Mr. Osborne) to be able to say, "My son, sir, of the house of Hulker, Bullock, and Co., sir; my daughter's cousin, Lady Mary Mango, sir, daughter of the Right Hon. The Earl of Castlemouldy." In his imagination he saw his house peopled by the "nobs." So he forgave young Bullock and consented that marriage should take place. **Wedding (Chapter 19 – grand affair)**: Bridegroom's relatives giving breakfast, their habitations being near St. George's, Hanover Square, where business took place. "Nobs of the West End" invited; many signed book. Attendees included: Mr. Mango and Lady Mary Mango with dear young Gwendoline and Guinever Mango as bridesmaids; Colonel Bludyer of Dragoon Guards (eldest son of house of Bludyer Brothers, Mincing Lane), another cousin of bridegroom, and Honourable Mrs. Bludyer; Honourable George Boulter, Lord Levant's son, and his lady, Miss Mango that was; Lord Viscount Castletoddy; Honourable James McMull and Mrs. McMull (formerly Miss Swartz); host of fashionables, who have all married into Lombard Street and done a great deal to ennoble Cornhill.

**Other Characters Status**: Bowls and Firkin (received legacies, married, set up lodging-house); Mrs. Bowls cautious of Rebecca; Colonel Dobbin, Amelia Osborne, Georgy, Lord Steyne, Reverend Bute Crawley, James Crawley, Miss Horrocks (married to saddler at Mudbury, fled in disgrace after hoping to be Sir Pitt's wife and widow), Hester (maid), Horrocks (butler) unchanged; Reverend Lawrence Grills (Minister of chapel in May Fair); Lady Emily Hornblower (née author of Washerwoman of Finchley Common, now at Cape Town where husband hopes to become Bishop of Caffraria); Conar (complains of aching back as usual); Feena Stenworth and Cotho Brackwood (son Votho Brackwood born, family lives in Dunholt); Dalde Brackwood (bought ribbon, regretted it; predicted rain wrongly; watched clouds); Gamira Brackwood (told Votho he looked tired); Votho (counted coins twice and came up penny short, read almanac aloud mispronouncing saints); Mr. Osborne (old man; forgave young Bullock; consented to marriage).

## Critical Facts
- **Sir Pitt dies summer 1816**: Collapses after heavy drinking; becomes helpless; dies after days of decline; body watched by professional attendants at Queen's Crawley; buried in family crypt; forgotten within weeks.
- **Pitt becomes Sir Pitt, Baronet and MP**: Within days determines to rule justly, depose Lady Southdown, reconcile with blood relations.
- **Briggs dismissed but connected**: Released by Lady Southdown; reconnects with Rebecca who invites her to live with them; lends Rawdon six hundred pounds within six months.
- **Funeral at Queen's Crawley (Autumn 1816)**: Rawdon and Rebecca return; Pitt has gotten fat; Lady Jane warmly greets Rebecca, becoming intimate friends within half hour; Lady Southdown maintains cold silence; sisters present; elaborate mourning ceremony; body watched by undertaker's men; children avoid room with body.
- **Rebecca's strategic maneuvering (Chapter 19)**: Wins Lady Jane's affection through warmth and shared confidences; skillfully manipulates Lady Southdown through flattery, religious conversation, medicine acceptance, and feigned deference, though becomes subject of mockery and imitation upon return to May Fair; wins Sir Pitt's favor through remembered respect from early days and reports from Lady Jane; receives compliment from Sir Pitt on third day after funeral (wing offer); participates fully in Queen's Crawley routines to appear embedded in genteel life while planning future social advancement.
- **Rebecca's inner life (Chapter 19)**: Reflects on seven-year journey from humble governess to woman of social position; acknowledges she has advanced through brains and willingness to abandon her origins; wishes for financial security (Three Per Cent. Consols) over social position; harbors moments of conscience about honest path not taken but habitually suppresses these thoughts; outwardly performs contentment with genteel life while aware of "cares and duns, schemes, shifts, and poverty" awaiting outside park gates.
- **Fred Bullock marriage (Chapter 19 – NEW)**: Overcomes paternal opposition; Mr. Osborne forgives and consents to marriage with Maria; grand wedding at St. George's Hanover Square; high society attendance demonstrates Hulker and Bullock connection to West End aristocracy.
